name: dvr-scan
desc: Extract scenes with motion from videos
why: Pulls motion-containing scenes out of video, a practical transform that is a close call for the catalogue.

brief.what_it_is: DVR-Scan is a command-line application, with a GUI launched as dvr-scan-app, that scans video files for motion, such as security camera footage. You give it one or more video files, and it finds the areas where motion occurs. It saves each motion event as a separate video clip. It runs on Windows, Linux, and Mac and is free and open-source.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames the problem as automatically detecting motion events in video files (e.g. security camera footage), so a person doesn't have to watch hours of footage to find the moments that matter.
brief.how_it_works: The README says DVR-Scan looks for areas in footage containing motion and saves each event to a separate video clip. Options include limiting detection to a region of interest (-r, or -a with a list of points), drawing bounding boxes around motion (-bb), and using ffmpeg to extract events (-m ffmpeg). The README does not explain the detection algorithm itself. Motion sensitivity is adjusted under Settings -> Motion in the UI, and many options can be set in a config file.

commands_seen.context: Quick install from PyPI, per the GitHub README.
Launches the graphical app; you then press Add to add videos and Start to run detection.
Scans video.mp4 and writes a separate clip for each motion event.
Scans only a region of interest, selected with the region editor (Ctrl + H shows its controls).
Selects the scan region from the command line using a list of X Y points.
Draws boxes around detected motion in the output.
Uses ffmpeg to extract the motion events.
Prints an overview of command-line options.

brief.install_notes: The README gives pip install dvr-scan --upgrade as the quick install. Windows builds, both an installer and a portable version, are on the Downloads page at dvr-scan.com/download/. The project does not mention accounts, hardware, or other runtimes beyond what pip needs. Optional ffmpeg use (-m ffmpeg) implies ffmpeg must be available, though I did not confirm the exact requirement. Some settings can be set in a config file, documented in the docs.
brief.standout: It is a dedicated tool for the 'find the motion in old footage' job, not a live camera system. It can also run its extraction through ffmpeg, and it offers both a CLI and a GUI with a region editor for limiting where motion is detected.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub README lists the latest release as v1.8.2.1 (May 9, 2026). The homepage lists 1.8.2 (January 18, 2026) as the latest version, so the two pages disagree slightly. I did not check the commit history or release list.
brief.caveats: The homepage and GitHub README give different latest-version dates, so treat the exact version as uncertain. The GitHub README says both 'All rights reserved' and 'Licensed under BSD 2-Clause', which is an unusual combination to check against the LICENSE file. I did not read the User Guide or Documentation pages, so detection-algorithm details, sensitivity tuning, and the full option list are unverified. The project does not state platform-specific limits beyond the three OSes it names.
